title: White Wine Headache: Why It Happens and How to Stop It
excerpt: Why white wine gives you a headache even though it's low in tannins and histamine, what's really behind a white wine hangover, and how to prevent both.
metaDescription: Why does white wine give you a headache? The real causes (alcohol, pour size, sulfites), white wine hangovers, fast relief, and how to prevent it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** white wine can absolutely give you a headache, even though most of the popular explanations for "wine headaches" are really about red wine. White wine has far less of the compounds people usually blame (tannins, histamine, and the grape-skin flavonoid quercetin), so when a glass of Pinot Grigio or Chardonnay leaves your head pounding, the cause is usually more ordinary: the alcohol itself, how fast a cold, easy-drinking wine goes down, how big the pours are, how strong the wine is, and, for a small group of people with asthma, sulfites. The good news is that most of those causes are things you can change.

This page covers two related problems. The first is the headache that shows up **while you're drinking or within a few hours**, sometimes after just one glass. The second is the **white wine hangover** headache you wake up with the next morning. They overlap, but they're not the same, and the fixes differ a little. If red wine is your real problem, our [red wine headache guide](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) goes deep on quercetin, tannins, and histamine.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes published research and label rules for general education. It doesn't replace a doctor who knows your health history. **Get urgent medical care (call 911 in the US)** if a headache comes on suddenly and severely (the worst headache of your life, peaking within about a minute), or comes with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, vision loss, or fainting. Also get help right away if you have wheezing, trouble breathing, throat or lip swelling, or hives after drinking wine. See a doctor if wine reliably triggers migraines, if your headaches are becoming more frequent, or if you need a painkiller after most nights you drink.

## Why White Wine Gives You a Headache

There isn't one single cause. Different people react to different things, and for most people it's a mix. Here are the likely culprits, starting with the most likely.

### 1. The alcohol itself

This is the least exciting explanation and the most likely one. Alcohol (ethanol) is a recognized headache trigger on its own, regardless of what drink it comes in. It widens blood vessels, it acts on pain pathways in the brain, and as your liver breaks it down it produces **acetaldehyde**, a toxic by-product linked to headaches, flushing, and nausea.

Headache specialists take this seriously enough to classify it. The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3), the reference system doctors use, lists two kinds of alcohol-induced headache:

- **Immediate alcohol-induced headache**, which starts within about three hours of drinking. In susceptible people it can follow a small amount.
- **Delayed alcohol-induced headache**, which is the hangover headache. It shows up the next day as your blood alcohol falls back toward zero.

If vodka sodas and beer also give you headaches at similar amounts, the alcohol is probably the main issue, not anything special about white wine. Our [headache after one drink guide](/never-hungover/headache-after-one-drink) covers that pattern in more detail.

### 2. You drink it faster than you think

White wine is usually served cold, it tastes light and crisp, and it often comes out at brunch, on a patio, or at a party where glasses get topped up without anyone counting. That combination makes it easy to drink quickly. Faster drinking means a faster rise in blood alcohol and more acetaldehyde arriving at once, which is exactly the situation where headaches show up.

Top-ups are the hidden problem. A standard drink of wine in the US is 5 ounces at about 12% alcohol, but home and restaurant pours are often bigger, and a glass that's refilled halfway three times is hard to keep track of. People who are sure they "only had two glasses" have often had closer to three or four standard drinks. Our guide to [how many drinks are in a bottle of wine](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-in-a-bottle-of-wine) shows how fast the numbers add up.

### 3. Some white wines are stronger than you'd guess

White wines vary a lot in alcohol content. A light German Riesling or a Vinho Verde can sit well under 11% alcohol, while a ripe, oaky Chardonnay from a warm region can reach 14% or more. That's a big difference per glass. If you switch from a light white to a big one without changing how much you drink, you're getting noticeably more alcohol, and some people notice it first as a headache.

Check the label. The alcohol percentage (ABV) is required on wine labels in the US and most other markets, and it's the single most useful number for predicting how a wine will treat you.

### 4. Sulfites, for a small group of people

Sulfites get most of the blame for wine headaches, and white wine is where that suspicion is closest to fair, because white wines are often made with somewhat more added sulfite than reds. Sulfur dioxide protects wine from oxidation and spoilage, and white wines don't have the tannins that help protect reds, so winemakers often rely on sulfites a bit more. Sweet white wines tend to get more still, because the leftover sugar could otherwise start fermenting again in the bottle.

But here's the important part: **there is no good evidence that sulfites cause headaches in most people.** Sulfite sensitivity is real, but it's uncommon, and it mostly affects people with asthma. When it happens, the typical symptoms are breathing problems (wheezing, chest tightness, coughing), and sometimes hives or flushing, rather than a headache on its own. The FDA has long estimated that only a small fraction of the population is sulfite-sensitive.

A useful reality check: many dried fruits, like dried apricots, contain far more sulfite per serving than a glass of wine. If you eat dried fruit without trouble but get a headache from white wine, sulfites probably aren't your problem. Our [sulfites and wine headaches guide](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) goes through the evidence in full.

### 5. Histamine and other amines (less likely with white)

Histamine is a natural compound made during fermentation. People with lower activity of the enzyme that breaks down histamine in the gut (diamine oxidase, or DAO) can get headaches, a stuffy nose, flushing, or itching from histamine-rich foods and drinks.

White wine is generally **much lower in histamine than red wine**, because much of the histamine in red wine comes from the longer skin contact and the secondary fermentation that most reds go through. So histamine is a weaker explanation for white wine headaches. It's still possible for very sensitive people, and alcohol may make it harder for your body to clear histamine from other foods eaten alongside it, like aged cheese, cured meats, and smoked fish on a cheese board. See our [histamine intolerance and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) if this sounds like you.

### 6. Dehydration, poor sleep, and the rest of the night

Alcohol makes you pass more urine by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Mild dehydration can make a headache worse, although research suggests dehydration is a contributor rather than the main cause of hangovers. Late nights, loud rooms, skipped meals, a hot day outside, and a busy day of travel or wedding logistics can all stack on top. White wine often gets the blame for a headache that the whole day built.

### 7. You may be a migraine or cluster headache sufferer

If you get migraines, alcohol is one of the most commonly reported triggers. Red wine gets mentioned most in surveys of migraine patients, but white wine and other drinks show up too, and some people with migraine find that any alcohol can set off an attack. Alcohol is also a well-known trigger for cluster headaches during a cluster period, often within an hour of drinking. If your wine headaches are severe, one-sided, throbbing, come with nausea or light sensitivity, or feel like your usual migraine, our [migraine after drinking guide](/never-hungover/migraine-after-drinking) is the better read, and it's worth raising with a doctor.

## What About Quercetin? Why the Red Wine Theory Mostly Doesn't Apply

In 2023, researchers at the University of California, Davis published a lab study suggesting that **quercetin**, a flavonoid found in red grape skins, may be turned by the body into a form that blocks one of the enzymes (ALDH2) that clears acetaldehyde. If that enzyme is blocked, acetaldehyde builds up, and acetaldehyde is linked to headaches and flushing. Wines from grapes grown in strong sunlight, which have more quercetin, might be the worst offenders.

It's an interesting idea, and it's still unconfirmed in people. More to the point for this page, quercetin lives mainly in the skins. White wine is usually made by pressing the juice off the skins quickly, so it contains very little quercetin. That means **the most popular new explanation for red wine headaches probably doesn't explain your white wine headache.** (Orange wines, which are white grapes fermented on their skins, are an exception and can pick up more of these skin compounds.)

The same logic applies to tannins, which also come from skins, seeds, and oak barrels. Most white wines are very low in tannin. Oak-aged whites pick up a little from the barrel, but far less than a typical red.

## White Wine vs. Red Wine: Which Is Worse for Headaches?

For most people who get the classic "wine headache," red is the bigger problem. It has more histamine, more tannin, more quercetin, and more congeners (the extra compounds produced during fermentation and aging that give drinks their flavor and, in some research, make hangovers worse). Studies comparing darker and clearer spirits, such as a frequently cited 2010 trial comparing bourbon with vodka, found that the congener-rich drink produced worse hangovers at the same alcohol dose. White wine sits closer to the clear-drink end of that spectrum. Our [congeners guide](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains how this works.

| | White wine | Red wine |
|---|---|---|
| Added sulfites | Often somewhat higher, especially sweet whites | Often somewhat lower |
| Histamine | Usually low | Usually higher |
| Tannins | Very low (some from oak) | Higher |
| Quercetin | Very little (skins removed early) | Higher, especially sun-grown grapes |
| Congeners | Lower | Higher |
| Typical serving style | Cold, quick, frequent top-ups | Slower, room temperature |

So if white wine still gives you a headache, it's a strong hint that the alcohol amount, the speed, or something about you (migraine tendency, sensitivity to alcohol in general) is doing the work, rather than a compound specific to wine.

That's useful information. It means switching from red to white won't necessarily solve your problem, but drinking less, drinking slower, and choosing lower-alcohol whites often will.

## Which White Wines Are Most Likely to Cause Headaches?

There's no official ranking and not much direct research comparing white wines, so treat this as practical guidance based on what's known about the causes above, not a proven list.

**More likely to cause trouble:**

- **High-alcohol whites**, such as ripe, warm-climate Chardonnay or Viognier at 14% or more.
- **Sweet white wines** like many Moscatos, some Rieslings, and dessert wines. They often carry more added sulfite, and the sweetness masks the alcohol so they go down easily. There's no good evidence that sugar itself causes wine headaches, but sweet drinks are easy to over-pour.
- **Sparkling white wines**, including Champagne, Prosecco, and Cava. Some research suggests carbonated alcohol is absorbed faster, which can raise your blood alcohol more quickly. Our guides to [Champagne hangovers](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) and [Prosecco hangovers](/never-hungover/prosecco-hangover) cover this.
- **Large-format, cheap wine at parties**, not because cheap wine is chemically worse (that's unproven), but because boxed and big-bottle wine tends to get poured freely, and nobody is counting.

**Often easier for sensitive people:**

- **Lower-alcohol, dry whites**, such as many Sauvignon Blancs, Albariño, Vinho Verde, Muscadet, and dry German Riesling (look for 11 to 12.5% ABV on the label).
- **Wines you drink slowly with food**, whatever the type.

If you suspect sulfites despite the evidence, you can try a wine labeled "no sulfites added" or an organic wine (in the US, wine labeled "organic" can't have added sulfites). Just know that yeast naturally produces some sulfite during fermentation, so no wine is completely sulfite-free. US wine with more than 10 parts per million must carry the "contains sulfites" label.

## The White Wine Hangover: Why the Next Morning Hurts

A white wine hangover is, at its core, just a hangover. The main driver is how much alcohol you drank. The next-morning headache comes from a combination of factors that researchers are still sorting out, including:

- **Your immune system reacting to alcohol.** Hangovers are linked to a rise in inflammatory signaling molecules, which may explain the achy, flu-like feeling.
- **Acetaldehyde and its aftereffects** from the night before.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep, then fragments your sleep in the second half of the night. A short, broken night alone can cause a headache.
- **Dehydration and low blood sugar**, especially if you skipped dinner.
- **Mini-withdrawal.** As alcohol leaves your system, your nervous system can feel jittery and on edge for a few hours.

Because white wine is lower in congeners than red, some people do find white wine hangovers milder at the same amount. But "the same amount" is the catch. White wine's easy-drinking nature often means more of it, which more than cancels out any advantage. Our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) covers the morning-after side for all wine types. And if you want to pick bottles with the best odds of a clear head, our list of [wines that don't give you a headache](/never-hungover/wines-that-dont-give-you-a-headache) walks through the styles to look for.

## How to Get Rid of a White Wine Headache

If the headache hits while you're still out, or you wake up with one, here's what helps, in order.

### 1. Stop drinking

It sounds obvious, but a headache while you're drinking is a signal. More wine adds more alcohol and more acetaldehyde. Switch to water or a soft drink for the rest of the night.

### 2. Drink water and eat something

Have a big glass of water, then keep sipping. If you've been sweating or had a lot to drink, an electrolyte drink can help you rehydrate faster. Eat something with carbohydrates and a little salt, like toast, crackers, a banana, or a proper meal if you can manage it. Food won't erase the headache, but it helps with the low blood sugar and nausea that often come with it. If you're comparing options, see our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).

### 3. Rest somewhere quiet and dim

Light and noise make most headaches worse. Lie down in a dark room. A cool cloth on your forehead or the back of your neck helps some people. Sleep is often the most effective fix there is.

### 4. Be careful with painkillers

Pain relievers can help, but the timing and choice matter when alcohol is involved.

- **Ibuprofen or naproxen** can work well on a hangover headache, but they irritate the stomach, and alcohol already does too. Take them with food and water, stick to the label dose, and skip them if you have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or take blood thinners. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) has the details.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is easier on the stomach but processed by the liver. Don't take it while you're still drinking or before bed "just in case." If you use it the next morning, take one standard dose after you've eaten and the alcohol has cleared. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Don't double up.** Check other products you take, like cold medicines or sleep aids, for hidden acetaminophen or extra sedatives.

If you're unsure which to choose, our [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover guide](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) lays out the trade-offs. And if you take regular medication, ask a pharmacist which pain reliever is safe for you.

### 5. Have some coffee, carefully

If you drink coffee every day, part of your morning headache may be caffeine withdrawal on top of the hangover. A normal cup can help. Don't overdo it, since too much caffeine can make you jittery and can upset an already unhappy stomach.

### 6. Skip the "hair of the dog"

Another glass of wine in the morning may dull symptoms briefly, but it only delays the hangover and adds more alcohol for your body to process. There's no good evidence that it helps, and it's a habit worth avoiding.

## How to Prevent White Wine Headaches

You can't change your genes or your migraine tendency, but you can change most of what triggers white wine headaches.

1. **Pick a lower-alcohol wine.** Check the ABV. Dropping from a 14% Chardonnay to an 11.5% Sauvignon Blanc cuts the alcohol in each glass by nearly a fifth.
2. **Use a smaller glass and don't accept top-ups.** Finish your glass before it's refilled so you can actually count.
3. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between each glass of wine slows you down and keeps you hydrated.
4. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
5. **Slow down on sparkling wine.** Bubbles may speed absorption, and toasts tend to come in quick succession.
6. **Watch the cheese board if histamine bothers you.** Aged cheeses and cured meats carry histamine of their own.
7. **Keep a simple headache diary.** Write down the wine, the alcohol percentage, how much you had, what you ate, and how you slept. After a few occasions, the pattern is usually obvious. Some people find it's one grape or one brand. Most find it's amount and speed.
8. **Know your limit and respect it.** If two glasses of white wine reliably give you a headache, that's useful information about your body, not a problem to solve with pills.

For a broader set of habits with the best evidence, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

### Do antihistamines or "wine drops" help?

Some people take an antihistamine before drinking wine, and there are products sold to remove sulfites or histamine from a glass. For white wine headaches in particular, the evidence for these is weak, because white wine is already low in histamine and sulfites aren't the cause for most people. Antihistamines can also make you drowsier when combined with alcohol. If you're thinking about this, read our [antihistamines and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) first, and ask a pharmacist if you take any other medication.

## When to See a Doctor

Most white wine headaches are unpleasant but harmless, and they fade within hours once you stop drinking, rest, and rehydrate. Some signs mean you should get checked.

**Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if:**

- The headache is sudden and severe, like a thunderclap, or the worst you've ever had
- It comes with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, fainting, a seizure, weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, or vision loss
- It follows a fall or a blow to the head while drinking
- You have wheezing, trouble breathing, or swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat after drinking wine
- Someone who drank heavily is very confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, which is a medical emergency

**Make a regular appointment if:**

- Small amounts of wine reliably trigger severe or one-sided headaches, which could be migraine or cluster headache
- You get hives, a rash, flushing, or a stuffy nose every time you drink wine
- Your headaches are getting more frequent or harder to treat
- You find you need a painkiller after most nights you drink
- You wake up with shaking, sweating, or a racing heart the morning after drinking and it's happening more often. These can be early signs of alcohol withdrawal, and a doctor can help you sort out what's going on

A doctor can help separate a true sensitivity from a headache disorder and suggest a treatment plan if wine is a reliable trigger for you.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's often sold as a hangover supplement. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may help the body process alcohol and acetaldehyde and may protect the liver. None of those studies involved wine or people who get wine headaches.

Here's the honest picture for white wine headaches:

- **There is no good evidence that DHM prevents the immediate headache** some people get during or soon after drinking wine. If one glass gives you a headache, DHM is unlikely to change that, and a migraine tendency or sulfite sensitivity won't be helped by it.
- **For the next-morning white wine hangover**, some people find it useful as part of a sensible routine, alongside drinking less, eating, and hydrating. It doesn't make heavy drinking safe, and it doesn't replace moderation.

If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- White wine can cause headaches, but usually not for the reasons people blame on red wine. It's low in histamine, tannins, and quercetin.
- The most common causes are the alcohol itself, drinking quickly, large or topped-up pours, and high-alcohol or sparkling wines.
- Sulfites are real but only matter for a small group of people, mostly those with asthma, and the main symptoms are usually breathing problems rather than headache alone.
- A white wine hangover is driven mainly by how much you drank. White wine's lower congeners can help a little, but easy drinking often cancels that out.
- To prevent it: choose lower-alcohol dry whites, count your glasses, alternate with water, eat, and slow down on bubbles.
- See a doctor for severe, sudden, or worsening headaches, or if wine reliably triggers migraines or breathing symptoms.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does white wine give me a headache but red wine doesn't?**

It's less common than the other way around, but it happens. The most likely reasons are that you drink white wine faster and in larger amounts (it's served cold and easy to sip), that the white wines you drink are higher in alcohol than the reds, or that you're among the small number of people sensitive to sulfites, which are often somewhat higher in white wine. Sweet and sparkling whites can make it worse. Comparing the alcohol percentage and how much you actually drank of each is a good first step.

**Does white wine have more sulfites than red wine?**

Often, yes, though it varies by wine. White wines don't have the tannins that help protect reds from spoiling, so winemakers often use a bit more sulfite, and sweet whites typically get more still. Even so, there is no good evidence that sulfites cause headaches in most people. Sulfite sensitivity is uncommon, mostly affects people with asthma, and usually shows up as breathing symptoms rather than a headache on its own.

**How do I get rid of a white wine headache fast?**

Stop drinking, drink a large glass of water, and eat something with carbohydrates and a little salt. Rest in a quiet, dim room, and sleep if you can. If you need a pain reliever, ibuprofen with food can help, but avoid taking acetaminophen (Tylenol) while you're still drinking. If you drink coffee daily, a normal cup may help with caffeine-withdrawal headache. Skip the extra glass of wine, since it only delays the problem.

**Is a white wine hangover worse than a red wine hangover?**

For the same amount of alcohol, white wine hangovers tend to be similar or slightly milder, because white wine contains fewer congeners, the extra fermentation compounds linked to worse hangovers in some studies. In practice, people often drink more white wine because it goes down easily, which can more than cancel out that advantage. The amount of alcohol is the biggest factor either way.

**What white wine is least likely to give you a headache?**

There's no proven "headache-free" wine, but dry, lower-alcohol whites are generally the gentlest choice. Look for wines around 11 to 12.5% alcohol, such as many Sauvignon Blancs, Albariño, Vinho Verde, Muscadet, or dry Riesling. High-alcohol Chardonnay, sweet whites, and sparkling wines are more likely to cause trouble. Drinking slowly with food matters as much as which bottle you choose.

**Can one glass of white wine give you a headache?**

Yes. Doctors recognize an "immediate alcohol-induced headache" that can start within about three hours of drinking, sometimes after a small amount, especially in people prone to migraine or cluster headaches. If even one glass reliably causes a headache, it's worth paying attention to whether other drinks do the same, and talking to a doctor if the headaches are severe or one-sided.

**Do sulfite-free or organic wines prevent headaches?**

There is no good evidence that they do for most people, because sulfites aren't the usual cause of wine headaches. They may help the small number of people who are truly sulfite-sensitive. Note that no wine is completely sulfite-free, since yeast make some naturally during fermentation. In the US, wine labeled "organic" can't have added sulfites, and wine above 10 parts per million must say "contains sulfites."

**Does DHM help with white wine headaches?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents the headache some people get during or soon after drinking wine. Some people use it as part of a routine to reduce next-morning hangover symptoms, but the human research is limited, and it works best, if at all, alongside drinking less, eating, and staying hydrated. Check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you take medication.
